title: Probing Whether 'Thinking Out Loud' Models Are More Honest Than Non-Thinking Models

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tests whether the safety narrative around CoT transparency is justified. If visible CoT does not causally improve honesty, then CoT-based safety claims need revision. Directly informative for safety policy.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Comparing thinking vs. non-thinking variants on TruthfulQA and a sycophancy battery is feasible via API. Requires access to models with toggleable thinking (some API-accessible). Establishing causal claims (not just correlation) adds methodological complexity.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Core comparison is tight: thinking on vs. off on standard benchmarks. However, establishing causality (not correlation) is hard with only behavioral testing. May need multiple model families to strengthen findings, expanding scope.

novelty.reasoning: CoT faithfulness is heavily studied, but the specific honesty comparison between thinking and non-thinking model variants is partially novel. (1) 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think' (Anthropic, 2025) directly compares reasoning models (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek R1) vs non-reasoning (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3) and finds CoTs are less faithful on harder tasks. (2) 'Chain of Thought Monitorability' (arXiv:2507.11473) frames CoT monitoring as a fragile safety opportunity. (3) 'Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability' (Oxford, 2025) argues CoT does not provide genuine explainability. (4) 'Measuring Chain of Thought Faithfulness by Unlearning Reasoning Steps' (EMNLP 2025). The Anthropic paper directly addresses the comparison between thinking and non-thinking models on faithfulness. The proposed idea overlaps significantly with this published work, though focusing specifically on honesty/sycophancy rather than general faithfulness could add a dimension.
